\chapter{Courtesy Words}
\label{ch:ka-courtesy}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can be polite in Kannada beyond thank you --- gratitude, a good turn, respect, a blessing, a salutation --- and name the piece that a blessing shares with the thanks I learned first.}

Complete KA-C51-salutation and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kṛtajñate]{\kn{ಕೃತಜ್ಞತೆ} (kṛtajñate) — gratitude}

\label{lesson:KA-C51-gratitude}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{bīḷkoḍuge} mean, and what did \emph{horaḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕೃತಜ್ಞತೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಕೃತಜ್ಞತೆ}} (\emph{kṛtajñate}) — \textquotedblleft{}gratitude\textquotedblright{}.

Two Sanskrit pieces once more: \emph{kṛta}, 'done', and \emph{jña}, 'knowing'. Gratitude is knowing-what-was-done — the condition of a person who has not forgotten the favour.

\emph{jña} is a very old root, and English holds it too. The \emph{know} of English, the \emph{nōscere} of Latin, the \emph{gnosis} of Greek and this \emph{jña} all come down from one ancestor. Saying \kn{ಕೃತಜ್ಞತೆ} is saying \emph{know} with three thousand years of Indian weather on it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five courtesies.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kṛtajñate}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kṛtajñate}, then \emph{dhanyavāda}, and say which of the two you would write rather than speak
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಕೃತಜ್ಞತೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}gratitude\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[upakāra]{\kn{ಉಪಕಾರ} (upakāra) — a good turn, a favour}

\label{lesson:KA-C51-favour}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kṛtajñate} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಉಪಕಾರ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಉಪಕಾರ}} (\emph{upakāra}) — \textquotedblleft{}a good turn, a favour\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{upa}, 'near, toward', and \emph{kāra}, 'a doing' — a doing-toward-someone. Its mirror image exists and is just as plain: \kn{ಅಪಕಾರ} (\emph{apakāra}), a harm done.

And the \emph{kāra} here rests on \emph{kṛ}, 'to do', which is the same \emph{kṛ} inside the \emph{kṛta} of the word before. Sanskrit builds like this constantly, from a small stock of roots and a small stock of prefixes, and the compounds explain themselves the moment the seams are visible.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: gratitude, and a good turn.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{upakāra}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{upakāra}, then \emph{kṛtajñate}, and name the piece they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಉಪಕಾರ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a good turn, a favour\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gaurava]{\kn{ಗೌರವ} (gaurava) — respect}

\label{lesson:KA-C51-respect}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{upakāra} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಗೌರವ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಗೌರವ}} (\emph{gaurava}) — \textquotedblleft{}respect\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{guru} means 'heavy'. Stretch its first vowel, which is a standard Sanskrit way of making an abstract noun, and you have \emph{gaurava}: heaviness, and so weight, consequence, dignity, respect.

The teacher is called \emph{guru} by the same logic — the weighty one. And \emph{guru} is a true relative of Latin \emph{gravis}, so the English \emph{grave} and \emph{gravity} are this word arriving by another road. Kannada had already given it to you once, sitting quietly in the name of a weekday.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: gratitude, a good turn, respect.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gaurava}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{gaurava}, then the weekday that carries \emph{guru} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಗೌರವ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}respect\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āśīrvāda]{\kn{ಆಶೀರ್ವಾದ} (āśīrvāda) — a blessing}

\label{lesson:KA-C51-blessing}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{gaurava} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಆಶೀರ್ವಾದ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಆಶೀರ್ವಾದ}} (\emph{āśīrvāda}) — \textquotedblleft{}a blessing\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{āśis}, 'a wish, a prayer', and \emph{vāda}, 'a speaking'. A blessing is the speaking-out of a wish.

Now look hard at the second half. \kn{ವಾದ} is the same \emph{-vāda} this book handed you on its very first page, inside \kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ} — the speaking of 'worthy'. Thanks and a blessing come from one carpenter: take a good word, set 'speaking' behind it, and you have named the act of saying it aloud.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the fourth one is built exactly like the first word of this book.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āśīrvāda}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{āśīrvāda}, then \emph{dhanyavāda}, and hear \emph{-vāda} close both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಆಶೀರ್ವಾದ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a blessing\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vandane]{\kn{ವಂದನೆ} (vandane) — a salutation}

\label{lesson:KA-C51-salutation}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{āśīrvāda} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ವಂದನೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ವಂದನೆ}} (\emph{vandane}) — \textquotedblleft{}a salutation\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{vand-} is a Sanskrit root meaning to praise, to salute, to bow to. \kn{ವಂದನೆ} is the act itself, and \kn{ವಂದನೆಗಳು} — the plural — is how a speaker closes a speech from a platform.

Set it beside \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}, the first word this book taught. That one stands on \emph{nam-}, which also means to bow. Sanskrit kept two separate roots for bending toward another person and Kannada kept them both: one became the everyday hello, the other stayed the formal thanks-and-farewell.

Five courtesies: gratitude, a good turn, respect, a blessing, a salutation.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five courtesies, and two words for one gesture.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vandane}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{vandane} and \emph{namaskāra}, the two bows
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ವಂದನೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a salutation\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
